claim: The Rising Star cave system is located within a small promontory situated to the south and east of the course of the Blaaubankspruit stream.
source: The Rising Star cave system, South Africa, is located within a small promontory situated to the south and east of the course of the Blaaubankspruit stream.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript describing the geographical location of the cave system.

claim: The cave system is situated within the dolomitic limestone of the Malmani Subgroup, a Precambrian marine rock bedded with chert bands and containing abundant stromatolite fossils.
source: The cave system is situated within the dolomitic limestone of the Malmani Subgroup, a Precambrian marine rock bedded with chert bands and containing abundant stromatolite fossils (Dirks et al., 2015).
evidence: Geological description supported by citation to Dirks et al., 2015.

claim: The Rising Star cave system includes more than 3 km of mapped passages comprising multiple levels within a west-dipping dolomite horizon.
source: The system includes more than 3 km of mapped passages comprising multiple levels within a west-dipping dolomite horizon.
evidence: Quantitative measurement of the cave system's extent.

claim: Abundant remains of Homo naledi occur within several localities in the Rising Star cave system.
source: Abundant remains of Homo naledi (Berger et al., 2015) occur within several localities in the system, including the Dinaledi Subsystem, which lies at a depth of ~30 m below the present surface and ~120 m through the cave system from the nearest present entrance (Hawks et al., 2017; Elliott et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The Dinaledi Subsystem lies at a depth of approximately 30 m below the present surface and approximately 120 m through the cave system from the nearest present entrance.
source: Abundant remains of Homo naledi (Berger et al., 2015) occur within several localities in the system, including the Dinaledi Subsystem, which lies at a depth of ~30 m below the present surface and ~120 m through the cave system from the nearest present entrance (Hawks et al., 2017; Elliott et al., 2021).
evidence: Specific measurements of depth and distance provided with supporting citations.

claim: Remains of H. naledi have been recovered and excavated from the Dinaledi Chamber, Hill Antechamber, and adjacent spaces and fissures.
source: Remains of H. naledi have been recovered and excavated from the Dinaledi Chamber, Hill Antechamber, and adjacent spaces and fissures (Berger et al., 2015; Berger et al., 2025; Brophy et al., 2024).
evidence: Statement about fossil recovery locations supported by multiple citations.

claim: The spaces in the Dinaledi Subsystem are challenging to enter and navigate.
source: These spaces are challenging to enter and navigate, and exploration of them is ongoing (Berger et al., 2025; Elliott et al., 2021).
evidence: Description of cave accessibility supported by citations.

claim: On July 28, 2022, engraved markings were identified on the southern and northern faces of a natural pillar in the Dinaledi Subsystem.
source: On July 28, 2022, during a survey of the Dinaledi Subsystem, we identified what appear to be engraved markings on the southern and northern faces of a natural pillar that forms the entrance and exit of a narrow passage connecting the Hill Antechamber with the Dinaledi Chamber (Figure 1).
evidence: Specific date and description of discovery with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The marks include linear features between approximately 5 and 15 cm in length.
source: The marks include linear features between ~5 and~15 cm in length.
evidence: Quantitative measurement of the markings.

claim: Many of the marks intersect to form geometric patterns such as squares, triangles, crosses, and X's.
source: Many intersect to form geometric patterns such as squares, triangles, crosses, and X's, while some are isolated lines.
evidence: Description of the patterns observed in the markings.

claim: The markings are located on three dolomitic panels on otherwise smooth areas, as well as in and around existing cracks and grooves in the rock.
source: These markings are located on three dolomitic panels on otherwise smooth areas, as well as in and around existing cracks and grooves in the rock.
evidence: Description of the location and substrate of the markings.

claim: The markings occur in three areas labeled A, B, and C.
source: They occur in three areas which we have labeled A, B, and C.
evidence: Classification system for the marking locations.

claim: The markings are in a location where they can be viewed during access into and egress from the Dinaledi Chamber when entering the system from the Hill Antechamber.
source: These markings are in a location where they can be viewed during access into and egress from the Dinaledi Chamber when entering the system from the Hill Antechamber.
evidence: Description of the visibility and accessibility of the markings.

claim: The Hill Antechamber is the likely point of access by Homo naledi to the entire subsystem.
source: The Hill Antechamber is the likely point of access by Homo naledi to the entire subsystem, and the passage is the natural linkage between the two main chambers of the subsystem (see Figure 1, also Elliott et al., 2021).
evidence: Inference about H. naledi access patterns supported by citation and figure reference.

claim: Panel A is found on the southern face of the natural pillar that forms the southern edge of the entry from the Hill Antechamber into the southern of two passages leading to the Dinaledi Chamber.
source: What we term Panel A is found on the southern face of the natural pillar that forms the southern edge of the entry from the Hill Antechamber into the southern of two passages leading to the Dinaledi Chamber (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: Specific location description with figure references.

claim: The most visible markings on Panel A are engraved lines, some of which when viewed together are cross-hatched and give the impression of a rough hashtag figure.
source: The most visible markings are engraved lines, some of which when viewed together are cross-hatched and give the impression of a rough hashtag figure (Figures 10 and 11).
evidence: Description of marking patterns with figure references.

claim: The lines appear to have been made by repeatedly and carefully passing a pointed or sharp incising tool into existing or new grooves.
source: The lines appear to have been made by repeatedly and carefully passing a pointed or sharp incising tool into existing or new grooves.
evidence: Inference about manufacturing technique based on observation.

claim: Several of the grooves on Panel A overlap geological features native to the rock, including fossil stromatolites.
source: Several of the grooves overlap geological features native to the rock, including fossil stromatolites (Figures 12 and 13).
evidence: Observation of relationship between engravings and natural rock features with figure references.

claim: It is possible to identify which lines were made first by examining the point where they cross another line.
source: In many instances, we suggest it is possible to identify which lines were made first by examining the point where they cross another line (e.g., Figures 14 and 15).
evidence: Methodological observation about determining temporal sequence with figure references.

claim: At least 46 engraved or altered marks are considered artificial on Panel A.
source: We identified at least 46 engraved or altered marks we consider artificial on Panel A (see Figure 16).
evidence: Quantitative count of identified markings with figure reference.

claim: There appears to be a temporal span involved in the creation of the engraved lines on Panel A.
source: There appears to be a temporal span involved in the creation of the engraved lines as some seem more recently engraved and show clean etching, while others have been obscured either by slight weathering or by the application of sediment.
evidence: Inference based on differential preservation states of markings.

claim: Some engraved lines on Panel A show clean etching while others have been obscured by slight weathering or by the application of sediment.
source: There appears to be a temporal span involved in the creation of the engraved lines as some seem more recently engraved and show clean etching, while others have been obscured either by slight weathering or by the application of sediment.
evidence: Observation of differential preservation states.

claim: The most easily identifiable engravings on Panel A, based on their clarity, are lines L2, L6, L9, L11, L16, L17, L27, L30, and L31.
source: The most easily identifiable engravings, based on their clarity, are lines L2, L6, L9, L11, L16, L17, L27, L30, and L31 (Figure 16).
evidence: Classification of markings by visibility with figure reference.

claim: Horizontal lines 11 and 25 on Panel A were created after vertical line 2.
source: While the existing lines may have been created in older etchings or been created over multiple interactions, the final etchings of the lines based on which lines overlap we interpret as follows: horizontal lines 11 and 25 were created after vertical line 2.
evidence: Temporal sequence interpretation based on line overlap analysis.

claim: Vertical line 6 on Panel A was created after L11.
source: Vertical line 6 was created after L11.
evidence: Temporal sequence interpretation based on line overlap analysis.

claim: Vertical line 18 on Panel A was created after horizontal line 17.
source: Vertical line 18 was created after horizontal line 17.
evidence: Temporal sequence interpretation based on line overlap analysis.

claim: Line 30 on Panel A was created after horizontal line 25, but before horizontal line 31.
source: Line 30 was created after horizontal line 25, but before horizontal line 31.
evidence: Temporal sequence interpretation based on line overlap analysis.

claim: Dolomite is known for a pattern of natural weathering that results in patterns of recessed linear features on its surface often called 'elephant skin' patterning.
source: Dolomite is known for a pattern of natural weathering that results in patterns of recessed linear features on its surface often called 'elephant skin' patterning.
evidence: Statement about geological weathering patterns based on established knowledge.

claim: Natural fissures and erosional features in weathered dolomite surfaces due to chemical weathering processes are characteristically deeper than several millimeters.
source: Natural fissures and erosional features in weathered dolomite surfaces due to chemical weathering processes (Burger, 1989) are in our observations characteristically deeper than several millimeters, and they follow natural fracture planes within the rock.
evidence: Observation about natural weathering features supported by citation.

claim: Natural erosional features in dolomite follow natural fracture planes within the rock.
source: Natural fissures and erosional features in weathered dolomite surfaces due to chemical weathering processes (Burger, 1989) are in our observations characteristically deeper than several millimeters, and they follow natural fracture planes within the rock.
evidence: Observation about natural weathering patterns supported by citation.

claim: Natural erosional features in dolomite may have variable cross-sections, ranging from beveled to U-shaped to rectangular in cross section with rounded or flat bottoms.
source: Natural erosional features in dolomite may have variable cross-sections, ranging from beveled to U-shaped to rectangular in cross section with rounded or flat bottoms (Jeelani et al., 2018) and are typically a few millimeters to many centimeters in depth, but do not have multiple parallel striations visible within them which would be characteristic of retouching or engraving.
evidence: Description of natural weathering features supported by citation.

claim: Natural erosional features in dolomite do not have multiple parallel striations visible within them which would be characteristic of retouching or engraving.
source: Natural erosional features in dolomite may have variable cross-sections, ranging from beveled to U-shaped to rectangular in cross section with rounded or flat bottoms (Jeelani et al., 2018) and are typically a few millimeters to many centimeters in depth, but do not have multiple parallel striations visible within them which would be characteristic of retouching or engraving.
evidence: Distinguishing characteristic between natural and artificial features supported by citation.

claim: Artificial lines in dolomite are limited in depth and extent due to the natural hardness of dolomite.
source: As opposed to natural surface weathering, artificial lines are limited in depth and extent due to the natural hardness of dolomite.
evidence: Explanation of constraints on artificial marking based on material properties.

claim: The hardness of dolomite means that any substantial artificial marking requires multiple parallel incisions with a hard tool.
source: This hardness (see Tabor, 1954) means that any substantial artificial marking requires multiple parallel incisions with a hard tool.
evidence: Inference about manufacturing requirements based on material properties with citation.

claim: Where artificial engraved markings intersect, they often appear to exhibit an ordering in which one was completed before the other.
source: Where artificial engraved markings intersect, they often appear to exhibit an ordering in which one was completed before the other (e.g., see Figures 6 and 13—15); this appearance of sequencing is not typical of natural weathering.
evidence: Observation distinguishing artificial from natural features with figure references.

claim: The appearance of sequencing in intersecting markings is not typical of natural weathering.
source: Where artificial engraved markings intersect, they often appear to exhibit an ordering in which one was completed before the other (e.g., see Figures 6 and 13—15); this appearance of sequencing is not typical of natural weathering.
evidence: Distinguishing characteristic between artificial and natural features.

claim: Previous researchers have noted the limited depth of artificial lines, their composition from multiple parallel striations, and their association into a clear arrangement or pattern as evidence of hominin manufacture.
source: In previous work, researchers have noted the limited depth of artificial lines, their composition from multiple parallel striations, and their association into a clear arrangement or pattern as evidence of hominin manufacture (Rodríguez-Vidal et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to established criteria for identifying artificial markings.

claim: The engraved lines in Panel A diverge in their patterning from the natural 'elephant skin' weathering of the surrounding dolomite walls.
source: The engraved lines in Panel A diverge in their patterning from the natural 'elephant skin' weathering of the surrounding dolomite walls, which can be seen adjacent to the panel within 20 cm of the nearest artificial marks (Figure 18).
evidence: Comparative observation distinguishing artificial from natural features with figure reference.

claim: Natural weathering features in the area of Panel A are deeper than 10 mm, maintain a consistency of size and depth across substantially undulating or rugged surfaces, and expand from natural cracks and fissures.
source: Our assessment of the features produced by natural weathering in this area is that they are deeper than 10 mm, in particular deep relative to the feature width, maintain a consistency of size and depth across substantially undulating or rugged surfaces, and expand from natural cracks and fissures.
evidence: Characterization of natural weathering features in the study area.

claim: Even the widest of the engraved lines that constitute Panel A have a relatively shallow depth.
source: In contrast, even the widest of the engraved lines that constitute Panel A have a relatively shallow depth.
evidence: Comparative observation distinguishing artificial from natural features.

claim: High-resolution macro-photography shows micro-striations constituting several of the engraved lines on Panel A, in which roughly parallel incisions sometimes overlap with each other.
source: High-resolution macro-photography shows micro-striations constituting several of these engraved lines, in which roughly parallel incisions sometimes overlap with each other (see Figures 6, 13—15 and 17).
evidence: Detailed observation from photographic analysis with figure references.

claim: Many of the lines on Panel A fall out of the direction of natural fracture features in the dolomite.
source: Many of the lines also fall out of the direction of natural fracture features in the dolomite, although it should be recognized that there are multiple places on this panel where natural lines and features of the rock may have been enhanced or extended by artificial engraving.
evidence: Observation distinguishing artificial from natural features.

claim: There are multiple places on Panel A where natural lines and features of the rock may have been enhanced or extended by artificial engraving.
source: Many of the lines also fall out of the direction of natural fracture features in the dolomite, although it should be recognized that there are multiple places on this panel where natural lines and features of the rock may have been enhanced or extended by artificial engraving.
evidence: Acknowledgment of potential interaction between natural and artificial features.

claim: Some of the elements described as engraved lines on Panel A appear to be artificial extensions or alterations of lines that may originally have resulted from natural weathering.
source: Some of the elements we describe as engraved lines appear to be artificial extensions or alterations of lines that may originally have resulted from natural weathering (Figure 18).
evidence: Interpretation of mixed natural and artificial features with figure reference.

claim: Panel A includes layered stromatolitic bands, and all engraved lines that pass below the bottom of line 14 cross over this fossil feature.
source: Panel A includes these layered stromatolitic bands, and all engraved lines that pass below the bottom of line 14 cross over this fossil feature (see Figures 13 and 15).
evidence: Observation of relationship between engravings and geological features with figure references.

claim: Where engraved lines cross over the stromatolitic feature on Panel A, they retain direction, and in some cases, the multiple striations slightly diverge.
source: Where engraved lines cross over this feature, they retain direction, and in some cases, the multiple striations slightly diverge, suggesting that maintaining a linear engraving over this irregular surface may have been challenging.
evidence: Detailed observation with inference about manufacturing difficulty.

claim: Maintaining a linear engraving over the irregular stromatolitic surface may have been challenging.
source: Where engraved lines cross over this feature, they retain direction, and in some cases, the multiple striations slightly diverge, suggesting that maintaining a linear engraving over this irregular surface may have been challenging.
evidence: Inference about manufacturing difficulty based on observed features.

claim: The markings on Panel A are, in places, covered wholly or partially in sediment or some other substance.
source: Second, the markings are, in places, covered wholly or partially in sediment or some other substance.
evidence: Observation of surface coating on markings.

claim: The coating on Panel A markings does not occur in other areas of the chambers where there are no such engravings.
source: This coating does not occur in other areas of the chambers where there are no such engravings.
evidence: Comparative observation suggesting intentional application.

claim: The material on Panel A may have been used to create visual contrast on the gray dolomite, to abrade the surface as a form of polish, to enhance or obscure some aspects of the engraved lines, or all of these.
source: This material (we cannot determine if it is sediment or pigment) may have been used either to create visual contrast on the gray dolomite, to abrade the surface as a form of polish, to enhance or obscure some aspects of the engraved lines, or all of these.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of possible functions of surface material.

claim: The material on Panel A is present on the surface as a thin layer and is evident within some of the grooves of the lines, indicating its application after some of the marks were made.
source: This material is present on the surface as a thin layer and is evident within some of the grooves of the lines, indicating its application after some of the marks were made.
evidence: Observation about temporal relationship between markings and coating.

claim: The appearance of time-ordering between engraved lines and the surface treatment may imply an origin of the engravings in multiple episodes.
source: The appearance of time-ordering between engraved lines and the surface treatment may imply an origin of the engravings in multiple episodes (Figure 6).
evidence: Inference about manufacturing sequence with figure reference.

claim: The covering on Panel A markings cannot be explained by geological or other non-organic processes.
source: Thus, it does not appear this covering, likely sediment, can be explained by geological or other non-organic processes.
evidence: Inference ruling out natural explanations for surface coating.

claim: The means of manufacture of engraved lines in the Dinaledi context would have required an implement of equal or greater hardness compared to the native dolomitic limestone.
source: The means of manufacture of engraved lines in this context would have required an implement of equal or greater hardness compared to the native dolomitic limestone.
evidence: Inference about tool requirements based on material properties.

claim: Dolomite rocks of appropriate size and morphology to mark the cave walls have been recovered from surface contexts within the Dinaledi Subsystem.
source: Dolomite rocks of appropriate size and morphology to mark the cave walls have been recovered from surface contexts within the Dinaledi Subsystem, as have many chert fragments.
evidence: Statement about potential tool materials found in the cave.

claim: Many chert fragments have been recovered from surface contexts within the Dinaledi Subsystem.
source: Dolomite rocks of appropriate size and morphology to mark the cave walls have been recovered from surface contexts within the Dinaledi Subsystem, as have many chert fragments.
evidence: Statement about potential tool materials found in the cave.

claim: Only one possible lithic artifact has been described in direct association with H. naledi remains.
source: At present, only one possible lithic artifact has been described in direct association with H. naledi remains (Berger et al., 2025).
evidence: Statement about artifact recovery with citation.

claim: The 'tool-shaped rock' found in association with H. naledi resembles tools from other contexts of more recent age in southern Africa.
source: This 'tool-shaped rock' does resemble tools from other contexts of more recent age in southern Africa, such as a silcrete artifact with linear engraved features on it that was recovered from Blombos Cave (Henshilwood et al., 2018; Figure 19).
evidence: Comparative statement with citation and figure reference.

claim: Panels B and C are located on the northern wall within 2 m of the Hill Antechamber burial feature.
source: Panels B and C are located on the northern wall within 2 m of the Hill Antechamber burial feature described in Berger et al., 2025.
evidence: Spatial description with citation.

claim: Panel B is situated lower and to the right (west) of Panel C.
source: Panel B is situated lower and to the right (west) of Panel C.
evidence: Spatial relationship description.

claim: Both Panels B and C appear to have been prepared in a similar way to Panel A, with possible use of cave sediment applied to the surface.
source: Both panels appear to have been prepared in a similar way to Panel A, with possible use of cave sediment applied to the surface, giving the surfaces of these panels an obvious textural difference to adjacent walls of the chambers (Figures 2B, C, 5).
evidence: Comparative observation with figure references.

claim: The surfaces of Panels B and C have an obvious textural difference to adjacent walls of the chambers.
source: Both panels appear to have been prepared in a similar way to Panel A, with possible use of cave sediment applied to the surface, giving the surfaces of these panels an obvious textural difference to adjacent walls of the chambers (Figures 2B, C, 5).
evidence: Observation of surface characteristics with figure references.

claim: A number of etchings and engravings can be seen on Panels B and C, some in the form of geometric figures, crosses, X's and one possible non-linear geometric figure.
source: A number of etchings and engravings can be seen, some in the form of geometric figures (Figure 7), crosses, X's and one possible non-linear geometric figure (Figure 5).
evidence: Description of marking types with figure references.

claim: A foreign substance appears to have been applied to part of Panel B in softer visible light.
source: It appears, in softer visible light, that a foreign substance has been applied to part of the panel.
evidence: Observation of surface treatment.

claim: The context of the markings within the remote Dinaledi Subsystem, far from cave entrances and challenging to access, suggests that the most parsimonious explanation for their manufacture is that H. naledi produced them.
source: The context of these markings within the remote Dinaledi Subsystem, far from cave entrances and challenging to access (Dirks et al., 2015; Kruger et al., 2016; Elliott et al., 2021), suggests that the most parsimonious explanation for their manufacture is that H. naledi produced them (Berger et al., 2015; Berger et al., 2025).
evidence: Inference about authorship based on context with multiple citations.

claim: H. naledi is the only species that left any evidence of presence in the Dinaledi Subsystem until the entry of modern cave explorers.
source: This is the only species that left any evidence of presence in this subsystem until the entry of modern cave explorers.
evidence: Statement about exclusivity of H. naledi presence.

claim: Linear features and other modifications of rock surfaces are sometimes produced by animal claws due to tunneling, climbing, or claw-sharpening, or other behaviors.
source: Linear features and other modifications of rock surfaces are sometimes produced by animal claws due to tunneling, climbing, or claw-sharpening, or other behaviors (Bednarik, 1991).
evidence: Statement about alternative explanations with citation.

claim: Deeply incised claw markings are sometimes seen in caves, which tend to include multiple parallel incisions with a spacing typical of the anatomical spacing between claws.
source: Such features have often been observed within caves formed within relatively soft limestone formations, including those in some parts of Europe and southern Australia. Deeply incised claw markings are sometimes seen, which tend to include multiple parallel incisions with a spacing typical of the anatomical spacing between claws.
evidence: Description of animal claw marks based on established knowledge.

claim: The susceptibility of a surface to marking by animal claws is determined by the hardness of the material.
source: However, the susceptibility of a surface to marking by animal claws is determined by the hardness of the material.
evidence: Statement about material properties affecting marking.

claim: Animal claws have a hardness of 2–2.5 on Mohs hardness scale.
source: Animal claws have a hardness of 2–2.5 on Mohs hardness scale (Rothschild et al., 2013).
evidence: Quantitative measurement with citation.

claim: Dolomite has a hardness of 3.5–4.5, with Malmani dolomites at the higher end of this scale.
source: Dolomite has a hardness of 3.5–4.5, with Malmani dolomites at the higher end of this scale, much harder than non-dolomitic limestones with hardness of 2–3, which are commonly marked by animal claws.
evidence: Quantitative measurement of material hardness.

claim: Non-dolomitic limestones have a hardness of 2–3 and are commonly marked by animal claws.
source: Dolomite has a hardness of 3.5–4.5, with Malmani dolomites at the higher end of this scale, much harder than non-dolomitic limestones with hardness of 2–3, which are commonly marked by animal claws.
evidence: Comparative statement about material properties and marking susceptibility.

claim: None of the cave systems in the Malmani dolomite have been noted for incised claw markings into dolomite itself of the depth and form seen in the Dinaledi marks.
source: None of the cave systems in the Malmani dolomite have been noted for incised claw markings into dolomite itself of the depth and form seen in the Dinaledi marks (Figure 17), even though clawed species like porcupines, honey badgers, and leopards do use caves and do dig into softer sediments found in the area.
evidence: Comparative observation ruling out animal claw marks with figure reference.

claim: Clawed species like porcupines, honey badgers, and leopards do use caves and do dig into softer sediments in the area.
source: None of the cave systems in the Malmani dolomite have been noted for incised claw markings into dolomite itself of the depth and form seen in the Dinaledi marks (Figure 17), even though clawed species like porcupines, honey badgers, and leopards do use caves and do dig into softer sediments found in the area.
evidence: Statement about animal behavior in the region.

claim: The hardness of the dolomite rock does not admit scratches by animal claws of the kind seen in the Dinaledi marks.
source: The hardness of the rock does not admit scratches by animal claws of this kind; additionally, the specific features of Panel A do not exhibit the kind of spacing or morphology that would be expected for repeated scratching by animal claws, and their position well above the cave floor would not lend itself naturally to scratching in that location.
evidence: Inference ruling out animal claw marks based on material properties.

claim: The specific features of Panel A do not exhibit the kind of spacing or morphology that would be expected for repeated scratching by animal claws.
source: The hardness of the rock does not admit scratches by animal claws of this kind; additionally, the specific features of Panel A do not exhibit the kind of spacing or morphology that would be expected for repeated scratching by animal claws, and their position well above the cave floor would not lend itself naturally to scratching in that location.
evidence: Comparative observation ruling out animal claw marks.

claim: The position of Panel A markings well above the cave floor would not lend itself naturally to scratching by animal claws.
source: The hardness of the rock does not admit scratches by animal claws of this kind; additionally, the specific features of Panel A do not exhibit the kind of spacing or morphology that would be expected for repeated scratching by animal claws, and their position well above the cave floor would not lend itself naturally to scratching in that location.
evidence: Inference ruling out animal claw marks based on location.

claim: There is no evidence of carnivore presence within the Dinaledi Subsystem: no carnivore remains, no evidence of carnivore burrowing activity, no coprolites, and no bones with tooth marks attributable to carnivores.
source: Further, there is no evidence of carnivore presence within the subsystem: no carnivore remains, no evidence of carnivore burrowing activity, no coprolites, and no bones with tooth marks attributable to carnivores (Dirks et al., 2015; Dirks et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement about absence of carnivore evidence with citations.

claim: There is no evidence of any hominin activity in the Dinaledi Subsystem other than H. naledi.
source: There is no evidence of any hominin activity in the Dinaledi Subsystem other than H. naledi.
evidence: Statement about exclusivity of H. naledi activity.

claim: No remains attributable to other prehistoric hominin groups occur in the Dinaledi Subsystem or any adjacent areas of the cave system.
source: No remains attributable to other prehistoric hominin groups occur in this subsystem or any adjacent areas of the cave system, nor is there any other evidence of activity of such groups (Dirks et al., 2015; Dirks et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement about absence of other hominin evidence with citations.

claim: Human cave explorers entered the Dinaledi Subsystem only within the last 40 years.
source: Human cave explorers entered these areas only within the last 40 years, and the number of modern cavers and archaeologists who have entered the Dinaledi Subsystem is extremely limited (Table 1).
evidence: Statement about recent human access with table reference.

claim: The number of modern cavers and archaeologists who have entered the Dinaledi Subsystem is extremely limited.
source: Human cave explorers entered these areas only within the last 40 years, and the number of modern cavers and archaeologists who have entered the Dinaledi Subsystem is extremely limited (Table 1).
evidence: Statement about limited modern access with table reference.

claim: There is no evidence of modern cavers altering cave walls in such a manner in the Dinaledi Subsystem, or elsewhere in the Rising Star system.
source: There is no evidence of modern cavers altering cave walls in such a manner in the Dinaledi Subsystem, or elsewhere in the Rising Star system, and we have detected no evidence of traces of metallic tools in association with the markings.
evidence: Statement about absence of modern alteration evidence.

claim: No evidence of traces of metallic tools has been detected in association with the markings.
source: There is no evidence of modern cavers altering cave walls in such a manner in the Dinaledi Subsystem, or elsewhere in the Rising Star system, and we have detected no evidence of traces of metallic tools in association with the markings.
evidence: Statement about absence of metal tool traces.

claim: Abundant remains of H. naledi have been identified within the Dinaledi Subsystem, including the Hill Antechamber Feature only 3–4 m away from the engravings.
source: By contrast, abundant remains of H. naledi have been identified within the subsystem, including the Hill Antechamber Feature only 3–4 m away (Berger et al., 2025).
evidence: Statement about proximity of H. naledi remains with citation.

claim: It is very challenging to establish the chronological age of engraved markings on rock surfaces.
source: It is very challenging to establish the chronological age of engraved markings on rock surfaces (Van, 1968; Butzer et al., 1979; Bednarik, 2002; Bednarik, 2008; Whitley, 2012).
evidence: Statement about methodological challenges with multiple citations.

claim: Successful use of geochronological methods for dating engravings may occur when some or all of the markings were buried within sediment that can be dated.
source: Successful use of geochronological methods may occur when some or all of the markings were buried within sediment that can be dated (Rodríguez-Vidal et al., 2014), or when markings were later covered in part by mineral formations that can be dated using radiometric methods (Hoffmann et al., 2016), or when exposure to weathering creates a varnish that can be dated (Dorn and Nobbs, 1992; Dragovich, 2000; Masson, 2006; Pillans and Fifield, 2013).
evidence: Statement about dating methods with multiple citations.

claim: Even where geochronological methods are possible for dating engravings, they may provide only a minimum age, which may be thousands of years after the marks were produced.
source: Still, even where geochronological methods are possible, they may provide only a minimum age, which may be thousands of years after the marks were produced.
evidence: Statement about limitations of dating methods.

claim: The markings identified within the Dinaledi Subsystem are not overlain by naturally forming sedimentary deposition.
source: The markings that we have identified within the Dinaledi Subsystem are not overlain by naturally forming sedimentary deposition.
evidence: Observation about absence of overlying sediments.

claim: Without further excavation of sediments that adjoin cave walls, it cannot be determined whether additional markings may exist in subsurface contexts.
source: Without further excavation of sediments that adjoin cave walls, we cannot say whether additional markings may exist in subsurface contexts.
evidence: Statement about limitations of current investigation.

claim: No obvious mineral deposition overlaps the engraved features in the Dinaledi Subsystem.
source: No obvious mineral deposition overlaps the engraved features.
evidence: Observation about absence of mineral deposits.

claim: At present, the H. naledi skeletal material provides the only information about the chronology of hominin activity in the area of the cave system where the engravings are located.

claim: The maximum age constraint reported on H. naledi skeletal material in Dinaledi is 335 kyr BP, which is the highest 95% confidence limit of a direct ESR-US date on H. naledi teeth.
source: The maximum age constraint reported by Dirks et al., 2017 on H. naledi skeletal material (335 kyr BP) in Dinaledi is the highest 95% confidence limit of a direct ESR-US date on H. naledi teeth; while the minimum age constraint (241 kyr BP) is based on U-Th on a flowstone that formed in part around a bone fragment (Dirks et al., 2017; Robbins et al., 2021).
evidence: Specific dating information with citations.

claim: The minimum age constraint on H. naledi skeletal material in Dinaledi is 241 kyr BP, based on U-Th on a flowstone that formed in part around a bone fragment.
source: The maximum age constraint reported by Dirks et al., 2017 on H. naledi skeletal material (335 kyr BP) in Dinaledi is the highest 95% confidence limit of a direct ESR-US date on H. naledi teeth; while the minimum age constraint (241 kyr BP) is based on U-Th on a flowstone that formed in part around a bone fragment (Dirks et al., 2017; Robbins et al., 2021).
evidence: Specific dating information with citations.

claim: The dates between 335 ka and 241 ka provide strong constraints on some H. naledi skeletal material from the Dinaledi Subsystem.
source: These dates provide strong constraints on some H. naledi skeletal material from the Dinaledi Subsystem.

claim: Geochronological methods do not yet provide similar constraints for H. naledi material from other parts of the cave system, including the Lesedi Chamber.

claim: The images on Panel A are not typical of contemporary graffiti made by recent people.

claim: The markings in the Dinaledi Subsystem are comparable to other hominin-produced markings, pigment use, and curation of nonutilitarian objects from the later Middle Pleistocene of southern Africa.

claim: Small slabs of ironstone with incised lines were excavated from Wonderwerk Cave, with a minimum age of 276 kyr BP.

evidence: Comparative archaeological evidence with multiple citations.

claim: One of the slabs from Wonderwerk Cave bears a series of seven roughly parallel engraved lines.
source: One of these slabs bears a series of seven roughly parallel engraved lines, while crossed lines occur on other slabs (Beaumont and Bednarik, 2013; Chazan and Horwitz, 2009).
evidence: Description of archaeological evidence with citations.

claim: Crossed lines occur on other slabs from Wonderwerk Cave.
source: One of these slabs bears a series of seven roughly parallel engraved lines, while crossed lines occur on other slabs (Beaumont and Bednarik, 2013; Chazan and Horwitz, 2009).
evidence: Description of archaeological evidence with citations.

claim: Beaumont and Bednarik, 2015 proposed that two sites in the southeastern Kalahari with open air rock engravings, Potholes Hoek and Nchwaneng, have highly eroded cupules dating to the early Middle Stone Age, possibly as early as 400 kyr.
source: Beaumont and Bednarik, 2015 proposed that two sites in the southeastern Kalahari with open air rock engravings, Potholes Hoek and Nchwaneng, have highly eroded cupules dating to the early Middle Stone Age, possibly as early as 400 kyr.

claim: Small pebbles of quartz, chalcedony, and other materials occur within the Wonderwerk sequence and have been interpreted as manuports.
source: Small pebbles of quartz, chalcedony, and other materials occur within the Wonderwerk sequence and have been interpreted as manuports (Beaumont and Vogel, 2006; Beaumont and Bednarik, 2013), although an alternative hypothesis that they were ostrich gastroliths, potentially introduced by hominins who hunted the birds, may also be possible (Tryon, 2010).

claim: An alternative hypothesis is that the small pebbles from Wonderwerk were ostrich gastroliths, potentially introduced by hominins who hunted the birds.
source: Small pebbles of quartz, chalcedony, and other materials occur within the Wonderwerk sequence and have been interpreted as manuports (Beaumont and Vogel, 2006; Beaumont and Bednarik, 2013), although an alternative hypothesis that they were ostrich gastroliths, potentially introduced by hominins who hunted the birds, may also be possible (Tryon, 2010).
evidence: Alternative interpretation with citation.

claim: Mineral pigments including specularite and hematite have been found in a number of contexts dating to earlier than 300 kyr, including Kathu Pan 1, Wonderwerk, and Canteen Kopje.
source: Mineral pigments including specularite and hematite have been found in a number of contexts dating to earlier than 300 kyr, including Kathu Pan 1, Wonderwerk, and Canteen Kopje (Watts et al., 2016).

claim: None of the examples of hominin-produced markings, pigment use, or other activities from the later Middle Pleistocene of southern Africa have been found near hominin fossil remains.
source: None of these examples of hominin-produced markings, pigment use, or other activities have been found near hominin fossil remains.
evidence: Comparative statement about archaeological context.

source: Some of them predate any evidence of modern humans or early Homo sapiens anywhere on the continent.

claim: The Dinaledi markings are comparable to some of the incised lines and engravings found at other sites in the later Middle and Late Pleistocene.
source: The Dinaledi markings are comparable to some of the incised lines and engravings found at other sites in the later Middle and Late Pleistocene (Figure 8 and Figure 9).

claim: Panel A gives the impression of overlapping crosses and lines that are remarkably similar in appearance to the engraving from Gorham's Cave, Gibraltar.
source: Panel A gives the impression of overlapping crosses and lines that are remarkably similar in appearance to the engraving from Gorham's Cave, Gibraltar (Rodríguez-Vidal et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparative observation with citation.

source: This engraving was dated to greater than 39 kyr cal BP and has been attributed to Neandertals.
evidence: Dating and attribution information for comparative example.

claim: The later Pleistocene record of southern Africa includes engraved bones and engraved ochre blocks from Blombos Cave.
source: In addition to the incised slabs and cupules mentioned above, the later Pleistocene record of southern Africa includes engraved bones and engraved ochre blocks from Blombos Cave (d'D'Errico et al., 2001; Henshilwood et al., 2002; Henshilwood et al., 2018) and lines impressed within sand features that were later lithified into aeolianites (Helm et al., 2021).
evidence: Archaeological evidence with citations.

claim: The later Pleistocene record of southern Africa includes lines impressed within sand features that were later lithified into aeolianites.
source: In addition to the incised slabs and cupules mentioned above, the later Pleistocene record of southern Africa includes engraved bones and engraved ochre blocks from Blombos Cave (d'D'Errico et al., 2001; Henshilwood et al., 2002; Henshilwood et al., 2018) and lines impressed within sand features that were later lithified into aeolianites (Helm et al., 2021).
evidence: Archaeological evidence with citation.

claim: There are a few other engravings from sites in Europe at similar time depth to the Dinaledi markings.
source: There are also a few other engravings from sites in Europe at similar time depth (Von Petzinger, 2017; Kissel and Fuentes, 2017, Kissel and Fuentes, 2018a), as well as geometric lines on a freshwater mussel shell from Trinil, Java, attributed to H. erectus based on geochronological considerations (Joordens et al., 2015).

claim: Geometric lines on a freshwater mussel shell from Trinil, Java, have been attributed to H. erectus based on geochronological considerations.

evidence: Archaeological evidence with citation.

source: The markings in the Dinaledi Subsystem share similarities with many of these geometric expressions from other sites and geographic regions.

source: Several geometric forms identified by Von Petzinger, 2017 are present, including cross-hatch, cruciform, line, flabelliform, scalariform, open angle, and oval.

claim: Many artifacts and rock walls from later Pleistocene sites with engraved marks appear to have a nonrandom placement of markings on an object or surface.
source: The precise location of the engraved markings within the Dinaledi Subsystem may be important to their interpretation. Many artifacts and rock walls from later Pleistocene sites with engraved marks appear to have a nonrandom placement of markings on an object or surface.

source: The broader record of engravings and other forms of meaning-making behavior in a range of hominin species and populations over the latter portions of the Pleistocene (Kissel and Fuentes, 2018b; Dusseldorp and Lombard, 2021; Kissel and Fuentes, 2021; Fuentes et al., 2025) suggests that such activity, be it 'symbolic' or not, was not exclusive to H. sapiens.
